item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The 343 and 682 interaction (or lack thereof) is pretty nice, and the interaction between Bright and 343? Solid as fuck.

"You have become an abomination Jack. More monster than human, bound to that thing." He gestured at 963, and I could have sworn I felt it tingle. "I should remove you from it, return you to your proper thread. Make you human again." For a moment, my thoughts lifted, hope at the thought that I might be rid of the curse, that I might finally die. But no. I clamped down on my emotions, refusing to break eye contact. He would or he wouldn't, but I doubted he could.

This, in particular, is excellent, and sets up both Bright and 343 so well as characters and individuals. Though ultimately, I'm not a fan of the first scene, even if it helps set the tone of the work throughout. So no-vote. Though I am reading through all of these.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
'Good' writing isn't necessarily the same as 'professional' writing.

Btw I'm in the same boat as you writing-workshops-wise - it's actually how I came here. The professor/author running the thing had us read the opening of John Dies at the End1, which I then bought, which I then looked up on the Internets, which led me to Slenderman which led me here.

Since you brought up writing workshops, I've got to say: I know negative feedback is much easier than positive feedback, and positive feedback isn't necessarily required at this site. But if you're going to critique Bright's writing style the way you would in a workshop, why don't you critique the story itself the way you would in a (good) workshop? Y'know, comments on the plot, structure, characterization, dialogue, even Bright's style overall (as opposed to a few snarky line edits)2. And positive feedback as well as negative feedback.

Either way, content, is much, much, much more important than occasional style issues or errors. Especially when the style works overall (which, I'd argue, it does, here).

Footnotes
1. This guy is one of the few workshop authors who pretty much reads - and is published in - every genre known to man, who will extoll the virtues of both New Yorker stuff and Shaun of the Dead.
2. I didn't do this because I'm lazy. But I also didn't go for snarky line edits.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Um,actually that is how writing works, at least good, professional writing. I've been going to writers workshops for years now, many conducted by multi-award winning authors and I can tell you that one of the things that they will always rail on first is telling the reader how the character feels when it should be obvious. If two characters are having an obvious angry argument then saying that the character said something "angrily" is just redundant. If the reader can't tell that the characters are angry by the tone of the conversation and the events leading up to it, then you're doing something wrong.

As per Caps lock screaming, have you ever seen it in a serious work of fiction? Eyes and Ellipses are just things that personally bug me because they are usually overused and often not effective.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I find this debate interesting because I've been in writing workshops for years now.

So here's my $0.02, for what it's worth.

I twigged on the capslock thing too but figured this was an entirely different format, so those things didn't matter so much. You want to severely limit use capslock in a published novel or short story, true, but this is a different format with different stylistic requirements.

You already addressed the stilted speech thing, but I wanted to say something about this:

Describing the tone with which a person speaks is unnecessary if the text is good enough. You shouldn't have to tell your reader the character is angry, the character should do that.

That's certainly true, but I disagree with the examples given. Dr. Samet is using mostly clinical language, thus it's not obvious from his words what tone of voice he's using. That's when you're supposed to clarify. It's not like this story went for a bunch of said bookisms.

Also, since I already started thinking about it: One of the things with grammar/style rules is that you throw half them out the window when it comes to dialogue. Dialogue is supposed to show character. If it's showing character, it's doing its job.

I'm surprised piecewise didn't point out the minor grammar errors (in the taglines - perhaps intentional, thus not even errors at all?), but either way, those don't detract from the story.

Which, by the way, is well-written and entertaining.

There is nothing wrong with having evocative eyes. If they were rainbow, or silver, yes. Emotive eyes, no.

I generally use ellipses for pauses, or trailing off. Just my thing…

sad eyes
flash of anger in his eyes

[adjective] eyes is what people do in fan fiction. It's not good writing.

"DR. BRIGHT! I do not need your negative attitude,"

Ditto on capslock screaming.

" anger in his voice."

Describing the tone with which a person speaks is unnecessary if the text is good enough. You shouldn't have to tell your reader the character is angry, the character should do that.

"I wish to again formally register my objections to this line of experimentation"

Numerous instances of clunky sentences. "Once again, I wish to formally register etc"

"…"

Ellipses should be used extremely rarely or never at all. There are better ways to denote pauses.

I think you mean "Gather Flies"
